According to the https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/bringing-you-agent-sandbox-on-gke-and-agent-substrate blog post, the substrate layer occupies a specific high-level position within the application architecture. This layer is designed to remain abstracted from the end user; instead, an agent application layer is constructed on top of it.

Consequently, for the Ax system, users should interact with the Ax platform itself rather than the underlying substrate directly. This architecture implies that the Ax system requires a front-end to intercept and process customer requests before forwarding them to the substrate layer.

We went through a similar transport decision building an A2A bridge. Started with gRPC, ended up adding SSE as a secondary channel because browser clients couldn't speak gRPC natively and the grpc-web proxy was one more thing to maintain.

One thing that surprised us: the bigger issue wasn't SSE vs WebSocket but **reconnection semantics**. SSE gives you `Last-Event-ID` for free, WebSocket needs a custom handshake. For a runtime that already has `last_seq`-based replay (#7), SSE's built-in resume might save a non-trivial amount of protocol design.

The WebSocket bidirectional advantage matters less when the protocol is already request-stream (Exec RPC), not true bidi.

Thanks for opening this. One downstream use case to keep in mind for trajectory exposition is that exposed trajectories may later be consumed by evaluation, replay, audit, or post-training pipelines.

AX does not need to own those downstream pipelines, but the trajectory schema could make them easier to build if it preserves a few pieces of metadata: model/harness version, tool/environment version or snapshot reference, verifier/evaluator version if available, trace completeness, replayability status, failure boundary, and artifact references needed for replay or audit.

FWIW I’d be in favor of keeping the OpenAI-compatible harness as a first-class AX harness rather than treating it as a special Gemini alternative.

A few compatibility details that tend to matter once people point an agent runtime at vLLM, OpenRouter/LiteLLM-style gateways, or other OpenAI-compatible endpoints:

- Treat `baseURL` as an exact API root. If the user provides `https://host/v1`, avoid appending a second `/v1`; if they provide `https://host`, either normalize once or fail with a clear message.
- Add a small preflight that tests both `GET /models` (or equivalent) and a minimal non-streaming chat completion. That catches wrong URL/key/model wiring before a controller run starts.
- Keep model/provider config at the harness boundary, not sprinkled through planner/controller code. That should make it easier for Codex or other harnesses to share the same config path later.
- For tool-capable controller flows, add one conformance test with `tools` + streaming if AX plans to use tool calls through OpenAI-compatible endpoints; a lot of endpoints are chat-compatible but fail only when schemas/tools are attached.

Disclosure: I’m associated with/evaluating KiroForge as an OpenAI-compatible multi-model gateway, so this is a use case I care about. Vendor-neutral support for `baseURL + apiKey + model` would be the main thing I’d want to validate, rather than any provider-specific integration.

@joycel-github, this is caused by the early failure if no Gemini credentials is set. Can you take a look?

Tried to reproduce the bug with some logs:
```
seq 21  toolCall get_weather(Los Angeles)
seq 22  stepUpdate STATE_ACTIVE  source=MODEL target=USER  text="The"          ← chunk #2 ("The")
seq 23  trajectoryStateUpdate    STATE_IDLE                                      ← idle fires HERE
seq 24  stepUpdate STATE_DONE    source=MODEL target=USER  text="The weather information for **Los Angeles** is currently unavailable."   ← the COMPLETE response, 1ms LATER
```

The localharness emits STATE_IDLE (seq 23) one message before the final STATE_DONE step (seq 24) that carries the complete answer. The antigravity SDK marks the connection idle on seq 23, and its receive_steps/response.chunks exits on idle + empty queue. So the harness's [chunk loop](https://github.com/google/ax/blob/e05fc43217060dcc09324175f7662f580b9167b5/python/antigravity/harness_server.py#L227) stops after the partial text "The" (seq 22).

We could have a defensive check on `conversation.last_response` after the harness's chunk loop. But the root cause is the race from the SDK.

## Fix

`Worker.processEvent` in `internal/controller/worker.go` dereferenced `task.Spec.Gateway.Name` directly (line 131) without checking whether `task.Spec` itself was nil. Since `ValidateTask` deliberately accepts a `Task` with no `spec` (it returns nil/no-error early on a nil spec), a metadata-only Task passes validation and then crashes the worker as soon as it's processed.

Replaced the raw field-chain access with the chain of nil-safe generated getters already used elsewhere in this codebase:

```go
var gw *v1alpha1.Gateway
if gwRef := task.GetSpec().GetGateway(); gwRef.GetName() != "" {
    g, err := w.store.GetGateway(ctx, task.Metadata.Atespace, gwRef.GetName())
    ...
}
```

This matches the same nil-safety idiom the file already uses for `task.Spec.WorkspaceRefs()` and that `ValidateTask` relies on.

**On the design question** — I can only answer as a reporter, not for the project, but having now read both sides of the boundary:

**Kubernetes RBAC on the port-forward path can't be the whole answer, because it doesn't cover the path that matters most.** `ax apply` reaching the server via `kubectl port-forward` (`internal/tunnel/tunnel.go:181`) does sit behind `pods/portforward` RBAC. But an actor or any other pod reaching `ax-server:8080` in-cluster never touches the API server, so no RBAC decision is ever made for it. That in-cluster path is precisely the one the original report is about, and it stays open no matter how tightly the CLI path is gated. RBAC-only would secure the door while leaving the wall missing.

Two further limits: `pods/portforward` is namespace-coarse and carries no tenant identity, so even on the CLI path the server can't tell *which* tenant is calling and therefore can't enforce per-atespace authorization; and it grants raw TCP to anything in that namespace, Redis included.

So the shape that seems to follow is **two callers, two mechanisms, one authorization model**:
- *Workloads/in-cluster*: mTLS with the SPIFFE identity Substrate already mints (`spiffe://${trustdomain}/actor/${atespace}/${actor}`) — the atespace is right there in the SVID path, so it binds the caller to its tenant with no extra plumbing.
- *Humans/CLI*: a Kubernetes-issued token (projected SA token, or the user's own credential) validated server-side via `TokenReview`, with the atespace bound to the validated identity rather than taken from the request.
- Either way the invariant is the same: **`atespace` becomes an output of authentication, not an input from the request body**, and the empty/`*` → global case stops being reachable for an untrusted caller.

That also mirrors what Substrate already does on its own API (mTLS creds + interceptors + the OpenFGA model in `cmd/ateapi/internal/authz/model.fga`), so AX would be adopting the model underneath it rather than inventing one. Happy to defer entirely to whatever the maintainers intend — mostly I wanted to flag that the RBAC-only option leaves the sandbox→control-plane path unaddressed.

Thanks for re-running all of that yourself — I agree with the deltas, and your read on the Workspace path is the sharper one. You also said it'd be good if someone with a working actor could settle the reachability question, so I spent some time getting one running. Here's what came out of it.

Short version: by default a sandbox cannot touch ax-server at all; give the actor an egress grant and it can — and the network layer knows exactly who it is, while the control plane doesn't.

A few details, since the middle part is where the interesting bit is:

- With no EgressPolicy there is no path. The worker logs `atunnel: egress gateway rejected CONNECT with 403 Forbidden: egress denied`, and the app-side read fails with connection reset. (The connect itself "succeeds" first because egress is redirected into atunnel — the denial shows up on the first read, not at connect.)
- With a policy in place, `GET http://<ax-server ClusterIP>:8080/` comes back with the server's own `404 page not found`. I get the same from an actor created by an AX task, not just a Substrate-created one. I also checked the host side as a control: that endpoint answers HTTP/1.1 and h2 prior-knowledge through a port-forward, so the 404 is the server's normal response rather than a transport artefact.
- Per-destination rules already work: a policy of `rules: [ - cidrs: {cidrs: ["10.96.89.38/32"]} ]` lets ax-server through and denies rustfs, the k8s API and the internet. So a grant can be written to exclude the control plane.

For contrast, a plain cluster pod doesn't need any grant: it gets 404 from ax-server, 403 `forbidden: User "system:anonymous"` from the k8s API, and 403 AccessDenied from rustfs. Every neighbour rejects the anonymous caller; ax-server has nothing that would.

How I'd read the severity, for what it's worth: what protects this today is the default of no egress, not an authorization decision inside ax-server. As far as I can tell nothing in the repo creates a policy (a grep for `EgressPolicy` across the tree comes back empty; the roadmap lists it as a goal). That default will change as soon as tasks need model or external APIs — and unless the grant is written to exclude the control plane, it is on the path.

One design thought, which I'd rather bring to #433 than grow here: the identity half already exists on the wire. The egress gateway logs every request as `peer_san=spiffe://substrate-actor.local/ateom-for-actor/<atespace>/<actor>`, with the CONNECT authority, and ax-server receives none of it. So "atespace as an output of authentication" looks less like something to invent and more like something to consume.

We maintain Containarium (https://github.com/footprintai/containarium), a self-hosted multi-tenant agent sandbox runtime that runs on both bare LXC and sigs.k8s.io/agent-sandbox on Kubernetes. Multi-tenant isolation on a shared control plane is our whole product, so the design direction this thread has converged on — atespace as an output of authentication, not an input from the request — is exactly the invariant we enforce, and I can confirm the shape works in production, not just in theory:
- Every RPC is scope-gated by a JWT validated before dispatch, at the handler layer, with no path that trusts a caller-supplied tenant field. (internal/auth in our repo — backend-neutral, ~101 call sites.)
- For the in-cluster/workload leg specifically, on our K8s backend we compile per-tenant egress policy directly into a native NetworkPolicy at reconcile time — the same primitive @bolubo's mTLS/SPIFFE proposal would sit next to. One thing that cost us a real incident to learn: a default-deny NetworkPolicy written once at object-create is not the same guarantee as one that's live-reconciled against current policy state. It reads as equivalent until a tenant's policy changes and the K8s object doesn't move with it. Given @bolubo's note that no EgressPolicy is created anywhere in AX today and the roadmap treats it as a future goal, it's worth deciding now whether that object is static-at-create or reconciled — retrofitting reconciliation later is more invasive than building it in from the start.
- Tenant secrets are materialized per-tenant with audit-on-read rather than stamped into shared config, for the same reason spec.env leaking across atespaces is the sharpest part of this report.

On the human/CLI leg: we landed on the same split — Kubernetes-issued token, validated server-side, tenant bound to the validated identity rather than read from the request — for the same reason @Aravindargutus gave: RBAC on the port-forward is namespace-coarse and carries no tenant identity, so it can gate the door but can't make a per-atespace decision.

Not claiming symmetry — our own audit trail is complete at the API layer but not yet for in-box sessions on the K8s path, and that's disclosed in our own docs, not hidden. But the "identity as output of auth, not input from the body" invariant is the load-bearing one, and it's cheap to adopt now before more of the Task/Workspace/Model surface (per #433) gets built on top of the current trust-everything default.

The core invariant here looks like requested lifecycle transition != confirmed lifecycle transition.

"SuspendTask" should not commit "Suspended" merely because the reconciliation path reached the suspension branch. The persisted state should be derived from evidence that the authoritative actor transition actually completed.

I would model the transition more explicitly as:

"requested -> dispatched -> confirmed"
with separate outcomes for
"rejected", "unknown", and "confirmed".

In particular, an RPC error such as "PermissionDenied" is a confirmed rejection, while timeout/cancellation may be an unknown outcome and require reconciliation against the actor's observed state before committing either "Running" or "Suspended".

A strong regression matrix would include:

- successful suspend -> persist "Suspended";
- explicit provider rejection -> preserve prior confirmed running state;
- already-suspended -> idempotent success;
- timeout after dispatch -> do not infer either state until reconciled;
- retry after an unknown result -> avoid issuing a second effect blindly unless the operation is proven idempotent or the current actor state is first checked.

The important property is:

a control-plane intent must not become an authoritative runtime fact without effect confirmation.

That also prevents downstream consumers from treating cleared worker identity / "Ready=False" as evidence that execution has actually stopped when the actor may still be running.

Even within those, rate limits and token budgets are very hard to manage, because output token usage is generally unknown and unbounded. A call's cost is only known after it finishes, and thinking tokens make it worse. So a token ceiling can only be a soft limit ("stop after the call that crosses it"), unless the call is metered somewhere the harness can't bypass, such as the egress gateway (#449). Per-tenant is really a grouping of the other budgets, so it probably belongs above a single Task.

On timing enforcement, @anudeep11k's server-side clock works at smaller scale. Three gaps to consider in the design:

Traffic can wake a task without AX knowing. Substrate's router resumes a suspended actor when a request arrives for it, and AX isn't told. The sweep only checks tasks AX has recorded as Running, so these runs aren't counted, and a task that already hit its deadline can run again with no limit. 

A failed suspend is reported as success. The reconciler logs a SuspendActor error and still records the task as Suspended (internal/controller/reconciler.go). 

Stopping tasks one at a time doesn't scale. If many tasks expire together (e.g. a burst of tasks created with the same deadline), the delay grows linearly: 10k tasks at a few seconds per suspend takes hours.

Thanks @MushuEE, these are all real gaps. Taking them in order:

**Tokens / per-tenant:** agreed. A token ceiling can only be soft (stop after the call that crosses it) unless metering happens at the egress gateway (#449), and per-tenant belongs above a single Task as a grouping of the other budgets. Time is the one budget AX can enforce exactly today, which is why I started there.

**1. Router wakes.** AX can detect these even if it can't see them happen: each sweep, call `ListActors` once per atespace and compare actual state with what AX recorded. An actor that's running while AX has it as Suspended or Failed starts the clock at the time it's observed (undercounting by at most one sweep interval), and if its deadline is already used, it's suspended again. That bounds the overrun but doesn't prevent it. Preventing it needs Substrate either to let the router refuse to resume a flagged actor, or to emit actor lifecycle events. Is either of those on Substrate's roadmap? If not, I can open an issue there.

**2. Failed suspend.** That's #441. The enforcer already treats a suspend error as "retry next sweep" and leaves the task Running (there's a test for it), so once #464 propagates the error, this path becomes correct for budgets too.

**3. Scale.** Two changes: (a) keep a Redis sorted set of Running budgeted tasks scored by projected expiry time (`runningSince + remaining`), so a sweep reads only tasks that are due, not every task; (b) suspend due tasks with bounded concurrency instead of one at a time. Total time is still bound by Substrate's snapshot throughput, but it no longer grows with the number of tasks sequentially.

Gaps 1 and 3 don't depend on how tokens or per-tenant budgets end up, so I'd like to own those: the expiry index, parallel suspends and wake detection, built against whatever time-budget shape you settle on. Quick update from starting on this. We're going to scope secret providers per atespace: a task just says which secret it needs (`secretRef: {name, key, inject}`), and the atespace decides where that secret lives through a `SecretStore`.

One catch on the Substrate side: the egress gateway only serves a single credential provider today. To actually let different atespaces use different providers (k8s Secrets for one, Secret Manager or Vault for another), we'd need either:
- multi-provider support in the gateway, routing on the `ate-secret://<provider>/...` host it already parses, or
- per-atespace gateways (the per-atespace gateway routing in the roadmap).

So for v1 I'm going with a `SecretStore` resource backed by k8s Secrets only, and a task that references a secret in an atespace without a store gets rejected rather than falling back to anything. The task-facing API shouldn't need to change when more backends show up.

Also worth raising with Substrate alongside multi-provider: the k8s provider looks like it resolves the Secret on every request, so caching will matter at scale.

It follows the fix suggested above. `spec.egress` on the Task lists the connections the task may open, as rules with one protocol each, `http`, `https`, or `tls`, with `hostnames` and optional `ports`; a rule without ports gets the default port of its protocol. The controller writes the rules to the actor's egress policy right after `EnsureActor` and before the first resume, which is the window that the suspended-by-default creation already provides, so the policy is in place before the task's first request. Tasks are immutable, so the policy is created once. The API server validates the section at apply time, as it validates names, and a task without `spec.egress` behaves as before. A refused policy fails the task with `EgressPolicyFailed`; an unavailable Substrate leaves it pending. Credential injection is left to #475, and the server flag for a default policy is left out so the change stays small; both build on this field.

Plan for this issue: just the runner-side change.

**Lenient decoding in the runner.** `pkg/apis/v1alpha1` gains `UnmarshalYAMLLenient`. It runs the same per-kind normalizers as the existing `UnmarshalYAML` methods, then decodes with `protojson.UnmarshalOptions{DiscardUnknown: true}`. `ax-task-runner` uses it for `AX_TASK_YAML` / `--task-file` and `AX_WORKSPACES_YAML` / `--workspace-file`. The existing `UnmarshalYAML` methods stay strict, so manifests applied with `ax apply` still reject typos and unknown fields. Blank or null YAML documents are still skipped, as before.

Leaving unused fields out of `AX_TASK_YAML` (part 2 of the proposal) doesn't apply upstream for now, since upstream has no `spec.egress` yet. Whoever adds the first control-plane-only field should strip it in the reconciler then.

What happens when a newer ax-server sends a spec with a new field set:

| New field is… | Runner before this change | Runner with lenient decoding |
|---|---|---|
| Used only by the control plane (e.g. `spec.egress`) | ❌ fails at startup | ✅ works |
| Not acted on by the runner (served by the metadata endpoint) | ❌ fails at startup | ✅ works (field is missing from `/metadata/v1alpha1/ax/task`) |
| Acted on by the runner (e.g. `WorkspaceSpec.files`) | ❌ fails at startup | ⚠️ starts, silently skips the feature |
| Rename / type change | ❌ | ❌ or silently wrong (needs a new API version) |

Known gaps:
- Runner images built before this change are still strict. Only images rebuilt after it get the benefit.
- When the runner should act on a new field, the failure goes from loud to silent: an older runner runs without the feature instead of failing. We can deal with that separately (e.g. a list of required runner features) if it turns out to matter.

Looking at it again, Substrate already covers most of it without anything new in AX. The router's CONNECT path can target any port in the actor; only plain HTTP requests default to port 80. What's left for AX is waking up cleanly. Substrate's wakeup probe calls the runner's `/readyz`, which reports ready before the agent's own server is listening again. So the first request after a resume can fail, even though the router held it until the probe passed. A small fix would be to let a Task name the port its server listens on, and have the runner's `/readyz` wait until that port accepts connections. +1. We've run both directions on our fork for a few weeks, on Agent Substrate v0.5 and now v1.0.0-rc.1, so here's what we learned in case it helps the design.

**Egress.** Ours is a list of host rules on the Task with injected credentials, which is close to the egress half here. Our triage agents call Vertex AI and the GKE API like this:

```yaml
egress:
  - hosts: [aiplatform.googleapis.com, container.googleapis.com]
    credentials:
      - header: Authorization
        prefix: "Bearer "
        credentialUri: ate-secret://k8s.io/default/ate-credentials/google-token/token
```

It has worked well. The agent never holds the token, and the egress gateway swaps in a fresh one on every request. Three things came up:
- +1 to the first open question. Nearly every task needs its model provider's rule, and we wrote it into every template by hand.
- Copying the rules into the actor's policy at create time is fine, but it should be documented. Changing a host list means re-creating the task, and someone will expect an edit to apply.
- Credential URIs name a Kubernetes Secret in Substrate's own scheme. Documenting the scheme next to the rule would save people a dig through Substrate's source.

**Ingress.** Until per-actor ingress lands in Substrate, the router's CONNECT path already reaches any port in the actor (my last comment on #501). The cluster-wide allowlist decides who can do that. On v1.0 any listed client can reach any actor: we list ax-server, our incident watcher, a dashboard, our e2e runner, and `kubectl ate proxy`'s atenet-client identity. So per-task `from.spiffeIds` would be a real improvement.

One thing the proposal doesn't mention, and the reason we kept a small patch: **waking up cleanly**. When a request wakes a suspended task, the router waits for Substrate's wakeup probe, which asks the runner's `/readyz`. The runner reports ready before the agent's own server is listening again, so the first request after a resume could fail. Our patch lets the Task name its server port and makes `/readyz` wait until that port accepts connections. If ingress rules list ports anyway, the runner could take its readiness port from there, or the Task could name it separately. Either would let us drop our patch.

**Naming.** `TrafficPolicy` reads well to us, and avoids both Substrate's "egress gateway" and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy.

When this lands, we'll move our fork's egress and port fields onto it.

## Live E2E check: Claude Code task image + mock Anthropic fake

We ran the Claude Code task image end to end on AX, using the `mock-anthropic` fake from agentexecutor/images#2 instead of the real API. These are the results and how the test is set up.

### Setup

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| Agent Substrate | `v1.0.0` (published images), gVisor sandbox class, 3-worker gVisor `WorkerPool` on GKE |
| AX | `main` @ 6887762 (`ax-server` + PostgreSQL, built from source) |
| Claude Code task image | `Dockerfile.claude-code` on top of the `ax-task-runner` image from the same commit; Claude Code `2.1.325` |
| Fake inference server | `fakes/mock-anthropic` from agentexecutor/images#2 @ a1a71b4, unmodified, running as a Deployment and Service in its own namespace, **outside** the sandbox |

How it fits together:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as Test harness
  participant AX as ax-server
  participant CC as Claude Code (runner, gVisor actor)
  participant E as Substrate egress
  participant F as mock-anthropic (in cluster)
  H->>F: POST /_mock/reset
  H->>AX: ax apply (Gateway + Task), ax resume
  AX->>CC: resume actor, runner starts claude --print
  CC->>E: POST /v1/messages (x-api-key from spec.env)
  E->>F: allowed by the Gateway http rule
  F-->>CC: SSE reply (MOCK_OK) or 401
  H->>F: GET /_mock/requests (count, auth_ok)
```

- **Gateway:** a single egress rule, `http` to the fake's Service hostname on port 8080. No allow-all.
- **Task:**
  - `spec.config` sets `prompt`, `model`, `maxTurns: 3` and `dangerouslySkipPermissions: true`.
  - `spec.env` sets `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (pointing at the fake) and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, a throwaway value that matches the fake's `EXPECTED_KEY`.
  - `spec.gateway` points at the Gateway above.
- **Assertions:**
  - The fake's request log: count, path, `auth_ok`, `key_presented`.
  - The runner's log line for the command exit, plus the Claude Code output.
  - The AX task state.

### Results

| Case | Fake request log | Claude Code | AX task state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Happy path (correct key) | 1 × `POST /v1/messages?beta=true`, `auth_ok=true` | Printed `MOCK_OK`, **exit 0** about 1.4 s after start | `Working` / `Ready=True` |
| Wrong key | 11 × `POST /v1/messages?beta=true`, all `auth_ok=false` | `Invalid API key`, **exit 1** after about **3 min** | `Working` / `Ready=True` |

What we learned:

1. **The image, the launcher, egress and the fake work together.** The narrow Gateway rule was enough. With `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1` (set in the image), Claude Code sent only `/v1/messages`: no `count_tokens`, no model listing, no side requests.
2. **AX doesn't move a task to `Completed` or `Failed` when its command exits.** Task state follows the actor's state only, so the task stays `Working` and keeps its worker until it is suspended or deleted. `runner.Config.OnCommandExit` exists but isn't wired to anything that reports the exit to the server. Until it is, "task reaches Completed/Failed" can't be asserted in E2E tests. This deserves its own issue.
3. **A wrong key doesn't fail fast.** Claude Code retried the rejected request 11 times over about 3 minutes before exiting. Every request had `x-stainless-retry-count: 0`, so these are Claude Code's own retries, not the SDK's. E2E time budgets for auth-failure cases need to allow for this, or the image should set a Claude Code retry limit.
4. **Scripted tool use, fault modes, the Vertex path, suspend/resume and gateway credential injection aren't covered yet.** They're next on the same setup.

We hit this for real, built a fix on our fork, and it has held up on three GKE clusters, so here's what we found in case it saves you some work.

**What happened.** GKE auto-upgraded our clusters on 2026-11-08 (RAPID channel, no maintenance window). Every task that was awake on a drained node died: its last condition said "worker pod went away while hosting the actor", and the task stayed failed. Suspended tasks were fine. It happened exactly as you describe: the runner stops the command on SIGTERM, nothing suspends the task, and the actor ends CRASHED when the worker goes.

**What we built,** on Agent Substrate v1.0.0:

1. **The runner stays up on SIGTERM.** On the first SIGTERM it keeps the task command running for a grace period (`AX_RUNNER_SIGTERM_GRACE`, 25 minutes by default, under Substrate's 30-minute window), so there's a live process to snapshot. A second SIGTERM or a SIGINT still stops it at once.
2. **ax-server suspends on drain.** Every 10 seconds or so it calls `ListWorkers`. For each worker in `WORKER_STATE_DRAINING` it lists the actors assigned to it and calls `SuspendActor` with `DURABILITY_MODE_SYNCHRONOUS` for each running task's actor. Synchronous matters: an asynchronous suspend can lose the snapshot along with the node. The task records why it was suspended, and its next request resumes it on another worker. One catch: listing workers needs global access, which runs into agent-substrate/substrate#3818 for an atespace-scoped driver.
3. **Two safety nets.**
   - An actor that still ends up CRASHED because its worker went away, say a Spot reclaim with about 30 seconds' notice, is reverted once to its last snapshot. Substrate only reports the crash reason as text, so this matches its worker-loss messages, which is fragile across Substrate versions.
   - An actor whose drain suspend failed, for example one whose runner had already exited, is also reverted once. That one keys on ax-server's own record of the suspend it attempted, not on Substrate's text.

   Other crashes are never reverted, so a task that fails at boot can't loop.

**Results.** We deleted the worker pod under an awake task with the default grace period. The task was suspended about 2 to 11 seconds later, and a request through the router woke it on another worker with its in-memory session intact. That passed on all three clusters, and it now runs nightly.

Things to watch for:
- the synchronous suspend holds the task's lock until the snapshot is uploaded;
- requests in flight when the actor is frozen are cut off;
- the bookkeeping for the safety nets lives in memory, so it's lost if ax-server restarts during a drain.

## Release steps for the first preview tag

Draft steps for the first tagged run, taken from `docs/releasing.md`, `release.yml` and the checklist above. They have not been run end to end yet. `PREVIEW_TAG` stands for the tag being cut.

### 0. Set the variables

```sh
export PREVIEW_TAG=v0.4.0-rc.1   # must match vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-PRERELEASE
export COMMIT=<sha on main>      # or on a release-* branch; any other commit is refused
```

A tag with a `-PRERELEASE` suffix is published as a pre-release and never moves `:latest`.

### 1. Before tagging

- `main` is green at `${COMMIT}`, including the nightly E2E run.
- `go.mod` pins the Substrate release to ship against.
- The person pushing the tag is on the bypass list of the `protect-tags` ruleset. Nobody else can create tags.
- A `google` org owner is available for step 4.

```sh
gh run list --repo google/ax --branch main --limit 10
git fetch origin && git merge-base --is-ancestor "${COMMIT}" origin/main && echo "on main"
```

### 2. Tag and push

```sh
git tag -a "${PREVIEW_TAG}" -m "${PREVIEW_TAG}" "${COMMIT}"
git push origin "${PREVIEW_TAG}"
```

### 3. Watch the Release workflow

```sh
gh run list --repo google/ax --workflow release.yml --event push --limit 1
gh run watch <run id> --repo google/ax
```

The `images` job pushes `ax-server` and `ax-task-runner` to `ghcr.io/google/ax`. The `release` job publishes the GitHub release. If `images` fails, no release is created. The image digests are in the job summary.

### 4. Make the packages public (org owner)

GitHub creates new packages as private. An owner of the `google` org sets `ax/ax-server` and `ax/ax-task-runner` to public in each package's settings, and links both to `google/ax`. Until then anonymous pulls fail.

### 5. Verify

Both platforms are present:

```sh
docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/google/ax/ax-server:${PREVIEW_TAG}"
docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/google/ax/ax-task-runner:${PREVIEW_TAG}"
# expect linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 on each
```

The release has the assets, and the manifest is pinned to the pushed digests:

```sh
gh release view "${PREVIEW_TAG}" --repo google/ax --json isPrerelease,isDraft,assets \
  --jq '{isPrerelease, isDraft, assets: [.assets[].name]}'
gh release download "${PREVIEW_TAG}" --repo google/ax --pattern ax-server.yaml --dir /tmp/ax-release
grep -n 'ghcr.io/google/ax' /tmp/ax-release/ax-server.yaml   # expect @sha256: digests matching the job summary
```

An anonymous pull by digest works:

```sh
docker logout ghcr.io
docker pull ghcr.io/google/ax/ax-server@<digest from ax-server.yaml>
```

The CLI installs and reports the tag:

```sh
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/google/ax/releases/download/${PREVIEW_TAG}/install.sh" | AX_VERSION="${PREVIEW_TAG}" sh
~/.ax/bin/ax version   # expect ${PREVIEW_TAG}; install.sh installs to ~/.ax/bin by default
```

`:latest` was not moved by a prerelease:

```sh
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/google/ax/ax-server:latest   # expect: not found, until the first stable release
```

A rerun builds nothing and records the same digests:

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --repo google/ax --ref main -f tag="${PREVIEW_TAG}"
```

`overwrite` is refused once the release is published (this run should fail):

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --repo google/ax --ref main -f tag="${PREVIEW_TAG}" -f overwrite=true
```

A manual dry run against the existing tag passes and publishes nothing:

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --repo google/ax --ref main -f tag="${PREVIEW_TAG}" -f dry_run=true
```

### 7. If something is wrong

A published release is never rebuilt. Fix on `main` through a PR, then repeat from step 0 with the next tag (for example `v0.4.0-rc.2`).

Walked the `ax local` path in the code (main @ af62e9da5) — a few observations that may shortcut triage. Code walkthrough only, no repro on my side, so treat these as the shortlist to check, not a diagnosis.

**What the error actually says.** `ax get tasks` sets up a background `kubectl port-forward -n ax-system svc/ax-server`; kubectl picks the pod behind the service (`app.kubernetes.io/name=ax-server`) and fails when its phase isn't Running/Succeeded. `Current status=Pending` means an ax-server pod exists but no container has started yet — that phase covers unschedulable pods, ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError, and stuck projected-volume mounts alike, so the message alone doesn't say which.

**Where the "hang" is.** The installer applies ax-postgres, waits (`kubectl rollout status --timeout=3m`), then applies ax-server and waits again (`internal/install/axdeploy/deploy.go`). A Pending pod turns that wait into ~3 minutes of "Waiting for deployment ... rollout to finish" followed by a bare timeout, and no pod events are printed. Note that an ax-server pod existing at all means the Substrate bootstrap and ax-postgres rolled out fine — only this last leg is stuck.

Fastest disambiguation:

```bash
ax local status
kubectl --context ax-local -n ax-system get pods -o wide
kubectl --context ax-local -n ax-system describe pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ax-server  # Events section
kubectl --context ax-local get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -40
kubectl --context ax-local describe node ax-local-control-plane | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/^Events/p'
```

Ranked for the single-node kind path:

1. **Pull of the user-supplied `--server-image`.** Everything else in the stack is digest-pinned from public registries; ax-server is the only workload with `imagePullPolicy: Always`, and `ax local` has no imagePullSecrets path, so the node can't use the host's docker keychain. Host-side digest resolution (`EnsureDigestPinned` in `internal/install/axdeploy/digest.go`) does use the keychain (plus a loopback-HTTP fallback for local registries), so a private or `localhost:<port>` image resolves on the host and then fails inside the node — the generated kind config carries no registry mirror, and unlike the e2e setup (`hack/setup-e2e-kind.sh`, which builds/pushes to its own local registry) there is no wiring for this. On Apple Silicon an amd64-only image lands here too ("no matching manifest for linux/arm64"). Events would show `ErrImagePull`.
2. **Scheduling headroom.** The preflight hard-fails below 4 GiB of container-host RAM but only warns for 4–6 GiB — with this exact failure mode in the warning text ("pods may stay Pending under load", `internal/install/executil/tools.go`). Events would show `FailedScheduling ... Insufficient memory` or an untolerated `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` taint.
3. **Projected volumes.** ax-server mounts a `podCertificate` volume signed by `podidentity.podcert.ate.dev/identity` plus a ClusterTrustBundle projection (`labelSelector podcert.ate.dev/canarying: live`). Substrate's own postgres exercises the servicedns/postgres signers but not podidentity, so this path is only proven at the ax-server layer. Events would show `FailedMount` — and the phase still reads Pending.

If it turns out to be #1, two small knobs would help independently of the environment: fall back to `IfNotPresent` when the ref is digest-pinned (a digest is immutable, and `Always` also defeats preloading via `kind load docker-image`), and dump `get pods` plus the failing pod's events when a rollout wait times out, so a hang becomes a diagnosis. **Design input: threat model and authz mapping against the current tree (af62e9d)**

Two things have moved since the September thread: the store is Postgres now (#419/#515), and the runner leg (:8081) already implements "atespace as an output of authentication" end to end. I won't re-argue the invariant; here is how the remaining decisions map.

**Threat-model layers.** Four caller classes need distinct principals: (1) tenant workload -> tenant workload (prompt-injected agent); (2) tenant workload -> control plane, where the amplification is the server's own authority — it resolves Secret references under a cluster-wide Role (deploy/ax-server.yaml:29-35) and talks to Substrate with a projected token, so an unauthenticated write is a confused-deputy primitive, not only a data exposure; (3) tenant operator -> other tenants over the port-forward path; (4) platform operator -> all atespaces, which today exists only as `atespace == ""/"*"` falling through to a global list (internal/store/postgres/store.go:158-164; server.go:147,797). Making (4) a positive cluster-scope capability preserves the admin workflow while removing the unauthenticated side effect.

**Authn, per leg.** The workload leg is already answered in-tree: Substrate's egress gateway mints a 300s Actor JWT scoped to `ax-runner` (internal/substrate/runner_egress.go:41-72), and runnerhttp verifies issuer/audience/exp and derives `ActorIdentity{Atespace,ActorName,ActorUID}` with a subject cross-check (internal/runnerhttp/jwt.go:54-58,140-224). Serving :8080 with the same verifier and a different audience would add no workload-side client work. The human leg is the open one: the public client still dials plaintext by default (client/client.go:96; its doc comment notes dialOpts are applied after that default), so a token or certificate source has to land there before :8080 can require credentials.

**Authz mapping.** RBAC-shaped, atespace-scoped roles cover CRUD cleanly. Two relations need more than verbs:

- *use/bind*: CreateTask referencing a Workspace/Gateway borrows that object's effect, so the check belongs at reference time — the gap k8s closes with `use`/`bind`.
- *reference-bearing resources*: Model carries SecretKeyRef (pkg/apis/v1alpha1/model.proto:40-43) resolved via ambient credentials (internal/model/client.go:270-295) while ax-server's SA holds cluster-wide secret reads; authorization should treat "which Secrets a Model may name" as an in-scope decision and scope the resolver explicitly.

ABAC/OpenFGA expresses *use* better than RBAC but adds a dependency; a middle ground is roles plus explicit bind checks.

**Egress / credential boundary.** The merged Gateway API snapshots rules onto the actor at creation (pkg/apis/v1alpha1/gateway.proto:42-46); that settles static-vs-reconciled for now, at the cost of non-retroactive revocation, which is worth stating as a boundary. Control-plane endpoints should be a destination class tenant Gateway rules cannot name (rejected at validation) rather than a CIDR each author must remember to exclude; the :8081 pattern — destination-scoped, audience-bound, short-lived token — composes with that.

**Audit.** The only RPC-level telemetry today is a StatsHandler with no principal (internal/server/server.go:96). Once authn lands, log (principal, atespace, verb, resource, allow/deny) and count denials separately: the deny signal is the security value, and cross-atespace list becomes an audited event rather than a default. Independent of authn, redacting spec.env / AX_TASK_YAML from Get/List responses (internal/controller/reconciler.go:270-276) is cheap and worth shipping first.

**Design input: what the current tree gives you, and the decisions this implies (af62e9d)**

Three current facts shape the request:

**Two credential models already exist side by side.** `Model.spec.secretKey` is name/key only (pkg/apis/v1alpha1/model.proto:40-43) and is resolved from Kubernetes by the client (internal/model/client.go:270-297). Separately, Gateway egress rules with `effects.replaceHeaders` inject credentials at the network boundary by reference: the `ate-secret://...` URI shape appears in the in-tree validation tests (internal/apivalidation/gateway_test.go:36-39), cleartext-http and wildcard-host credential rules are rejected (internal/apivalidation/gateway.go:43-52), and a Kind E2E covers the path (#588). The hero demo uses exactly this (hack/hero-demo/task-starter.yaml:38 — a placeholder replaced by the bound Gateway). Under that pattern the sandbox never holds the key and rotation is a Gateway edit, not a task restart. What that pattern does not carry is per-tenant model metadata — model name, generation parameters — which is the part worth adding to ModelSpec.

**The missing Secret namespace is currently the access boundary.** Resolution uses the Model's atespace as the Kubernetes namespace (internal/model/client.go:288-291), while the ax-server SA holds cluster-wide `secrets get/list/watch` (deploy/ax-server.yaml:29-35). Adding `secretKey.namespace` without a scope rule makes every Model a cross-namespace reference that the component resolving it — under that Role — can read. A narrow default (resolve only in the Model's atespace namespace, and make any other namespace an explicit allowlisted case with its own error) preserves the kagent-style use case and keeps "respects RBAC" meaningful. The same applies to custom endpoints: `baseURL` is a client option today (internal/model/client.go:71,208-212), not a ModelSpec field, so endpoint validation has no server-side home yet.

**Rotation and errors are the weak points of the Model path.** Keys resolve once at client construction (internal/model/client.go:262-265), so long-lived consumers pin credentials until restart. The only implemented call path is Google's, which sends the key in the URL query string (internal/model/client.go:509); for custom endpoints, header-based auth or gateway injection keeps credentials out of URLs and logs. And docs already show `provider: anthropic` (docs/manifests.md:285-304) while the client rejects anything non-google as "unsupported provider" (internal/model/client.go:486-495); `ValidateModel` today checks only metadata (internal/apivalidation/model.go:22-26), so provider/endpoint validation at write time would make the "actionable errors" expectation real before a task spends a boot cycle discovering it.

Consistency note: TaskSpec and WorkspaceSetup have no Model reference (pkg/apis/v1alpha1/workspace.proto:69-86), so whichever mechanism wins still needs an answer for "who resolves the Model for a given task run" — today it is whoever constructs the client.

**Design input: discovery-plane semantics and binding consistency (af62e9d)**

The metadata listener already serves loopback-only `/metadata/v1alpha1/ax/{task,workspace,goal}` (internal/metadata/server.go:125-131), so option 1 fits exactly. Four constraints:

**A provider-format `/v1/models` only works on a base that also serves inference.** OpenAI and Anthropic return different list shapes, and SDKs use one base URL for both `models.list()` and the completion call. If the runner serves `/v1/models` in a provider's format (option 2) while inference goes direct to the provider, discovery succeeds against loopback and the next call fails there — the harness needs two bases. So either the surface is AX-native with shims left to harnesses (option 1), or the serving base also proxies inference (option 3).

**Say when the list is resolved.** Tasks are immutable and Gateway rules snapshot at create (gateway.proto:42-46), while Workspace `spec.mcp` is resolved on every wakeup (workspace.proto:46-48). Document whichever. A create-time snapshot of (alias, provider, model ID, endpoint, credential ref) matches egress injection, which is also per-actor at create. Aliases (`default`, `fast`) should come from the spec, not positional order, and the list should carry both alias and provider model ID — without a proxy the agent can only call the provider ID. Label-selector binding works if the resolved set is recorded at create.

**Catalog vs policy.** A bound list is a catalog; fallback on 429/5xx is a policy. Option 1 leaves fallback to the harness, so the spec should not appear to guarantee it. If fallback is in scope it belongs with the proxy, which is also where per-model usage/cost attribution lives; direct calls leave a task dimension but no model dimension in telemetry (#471 inherits that gap). One optional capability field per entry (context window, tools) is cheap now: OpenAI's list has none, shims can ignore it, and agents can then pick cheap vs strong.

**Validate the binding at create.** #475's "one task cannot use two credentials for the same host" is a CreateTask check: two entries resolving to one host with different credentials should fail with an actionable error, not on first request; a provider-shaped `Model` sidesteps most of it.

On the second axis: nothing in-tree consumes `Model` outside its own package (the CLI does CRUD only), so a list/rename change is cheapest now; #563 marks Models "unchanged for MVP" while Task spec is still open, so this field lands in that window — and its AIP pass (plural fields, paginated lists) is the shape to follow.

Tracked down the root causes for this on `main` (`0b44e97`) and put together a tested fix + deterministic reproduction test on [`ghchinoy:fix/ssh-hang-653`](https://github.com/google/ax/compare/main...ghchinoy:ax:fix/ssh-hang-653) (commit [`bd2ff4d`](https://github.com/ghchinoy/ax/commit/bd2ff4d)):

### Root Causes Found

1. **`tunnel.PortForward` stdout/stderr pipe deadlock mid-session (`internal/tunnel/tunnel.go:463-488`):**
   `PortForward` uses a `portChan` of buffer size `1` (read once on startup) and re-evaluates `portForwardRegex.FindStringSubmatch(output.String())` on **every** subsequent chunk read from `kubectl`'s combined stdout/stderr pipe without stopping after sending the port.
   - Read 1 (`Forwarding from 127.0.0.1:<port> -> 443`) sends `p` and is consumed by the caller.
   - Read 2 (`Forwarding from [::1]:<port> -> 443`) matches the accumulated `output` buffer again and fills `portChan` (`cap=1`).
   - Read 3 (`Handling connection for <port>`) matches `output.String()` again and **deadlocks the reader goroutine permanently on `portChan <- p`**.
   Once `kubectl port-forward` writes past the ~64 KiB OS pipe buffer during an active session, `kubectl` blocks inside `write()` in the kernel and freezes the `ax ssh` tunnel completely.
2. **Double `Ctrl-C` / hangup skips `cleanup()` and leaks `kubectl port-forward` (`cmd/ax/main.go:1148-1152` & `internal/tunnel/tunnel.go:490-496`):**
   - `escalateInterrupts` calls `os.Exit(130)` directly, bypassing `defer cleanup()` and leaving the `kubectl port-forward` process group alive in the background until killed manually, and `cleanup()` never called `cmd.Wait()` to reap the child.
   - `dialRouterTLS` / `dialGuest` used `context.Background()` (so interrupts during `PodCertificateRequest` / port-forward setup exited before `defer cleanup()` was registered), and `SIGTERM`/`SIGHUP` were unhandled.
3. **No gRPC keepalive on active guest streams (`internal/guest/client.go`):**
   Added `keepalive.ClientParameters` (`Time: 30s`, `Timeout: 10s`, `PermitWithoutStream: false`) so silently dead tunnels are detected during active `Exec` streams without sending pings while idle.

### Ready Fix (`+204 / -32`, passes `make verify` & `go test -race ./...`)

- **Diff against `main`:** https://github.com/google/ax/compare/main...ghchinoy:ax:fix/ssh-hang-653
- Includes `TestPortForwardDrainsPipeAndReapsChild` (`internal/tunnel/tunnel_test.go`), which reproduces the >64 KiB `Handling connection for ...` pipe deadlock deterministically and verifies child reaping (`ESRCH`), plus `TestEscalateInterruptsExitsImmediatelyOnSIGTERMAndSIGHUP`.

Looking at `internal/install/` and `hack/build-local-cluster.sh` on `0bbe4f6` alongside my local testing with rootless Podman and macOS Apple `container`, there are four concrete spots worth addressing for Kind-based `ax local start`, plus a structural limit on macOS:

### Kind-based `ax local start` (Podman on Linux & macOS)

1. **Engine probe order mismatch (`Makefile` / `hack/` vs. `ax local`):** `Makefile` and `hack/build-local-cluster.sh` prefer `podman` first (`command -v podman || command -v docker`), while `executil.ResolveContainerRuntime` (`internal/install/executil/tools.go:138-151`) probes `docker` first, then `podman`. If both daemons are running and `CONTAINER_CLI` isn't set, `build-local-cluster.sh` starts the local registry in Podman while `ax local start` targets Docker and fails when attaching the registry container.
2. **macOS "no engine running" message (`internal/install/executil/tools.go:153-155`):** Currently suggests only OrbStack, Docker Desktop, or Colima—adding `podman machine` there (and noting `--memory 8192` alongside `--rootful` since `podman machine init` defaults to rootless 2 GiB RAM) avoids back-to-back preflight failures.
3. **Unconditional rootless rejection (`internal/install/executil/tools.go:223-228`):** `ValidateContainerHost` blocks `info.Rootless` on both Linux and macOS. On Linux, Kind (`KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER=podman`) supports rootless Podman when systemd cgroup v2 delegation (`Delegate=yes` for `cpu cpuset io memory pids`) is enabled (`net.ipv4.conf.all.proxy_arp=1` is per-netns); the main thing to verify is whether Substrate's `atelet` (`runsc` `systrap` + OverlayFS `lowerdir+` on kernel >= 6.8) starts cleanly inside that rootless user namespace. On macOS, default `podman machine` (`libkrun` rootless) still needs `--rootful` when running Kind + `atelet`.
4. **Rootless Podman 5+ `network connect` caveat (`internal/install/cluster/registry.go:105-110`):** Under rootless Podman 5+, containers without an explicit `--network` default to `pasta` rather than a netavark bridge, so `podman network connect kind <registry>` fails on a default-network registry container unless it is created on a bridge network (e.g. `--network bridge` or `--network kind`).

### Zero-Kind / truly rootless local option

Even with Podman polished, Kind-based `ax local` still requires a 6–8 GiB Linux VM, kernel >= 6.8, and rootful mode on macOS, and cannot use macOS native Apple `container` (`Virtualization.framework`). For a zero-Docker, zero-rootful local runtime on macOS/Linux, I've been maintaining `ate-local` (tracked in #602), which implements `ateapi/v1.ControlServer` + an embedded `atenet-router` directly over Apple `container` or rootless `podman` (`-p 127.0.0.1::<port>`) and runs `./hack/tour.sh` (#753) end-to-end without Kind (trading off `atenet-egress` L7 filtering / Kubernetes Secret injection).

Answering the four unknowns from the logs and kubelet events:

- Image pulls: Kind already pulls 4 images in parallel, so all 18 pod images overlapped into ~21s on a fast link. On slower links the ~1.20 GB total (+914 MB for the Kind node if uncached) adds up fast, and making the optional telemetry stack opt-in (285 MB) plus aligning AX onto Postgres 18 instead of 17 (117 MB) trims about a third of that.
- Readiness waits that could overlap: AX Postgres has no Substrate dependency ([deploy/postgres.yaml](https://github.com/google/ax/blob/651fd23/deploy/postgres.yaml)), so starting it earlier overlaps its 14s behind Substrate. The biggest non-pull waits are Kind node readiness (~21s), trust bundles (~10s), and local-path PVC setup (4 to 5s each).
- WorkerPool: not a bottleneck, taking 2.9s locally (1.9 - 4.0s in CI).
- Polling intervals: rollout waits already use Kubernetes watches ([rollout.go:84](https://github.com/google/ax/blob/651fd23/internal/install/executil/rollout.go#L84)) and print pod status every 15s, with only two small polling loops (1s and 2s).
